470.t: A year at Arthur Jordan Conservatory and being sent away from Butler
470.s: After high school he spent a year at Butler's Arthur Jordan Conservatory, was expelled for dancing with a white girl, and Dr. Roscoe Polin helped him enter Indiana University.
470.ch: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
470.q: I graduated, and I went there one year and met a lot of people who would be – because at that time they took a quota as far as blacks. I went there. It was Oliver Bell, Jimmy Coe, Trili Stewart, Reginald Duvall. I never got to play in the big – they had a big jazz band which was really quite good.…

470.t: Lincoln campus life: overheard remarks, a jazz concert and dating rules
470.s: He overheard teachers mocking him in the cafeteria line, staged a jazz concert, and learned the school's sundown rules for dating.
470.ch: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
470.q: Day-o. I did – the teachers were all doing – they were doing their whole acts, and I was in [the show] with the shirt tied around and . . . I chased everything. They told me who I could date, because I was single. They said I could date anybody who was a senior. Now at the colored schools at that…

234.t: Raising the sons; private school scholarship; being called black
234.s: Gil says his sons have faced little prejudice at a private school that gave them a scholarship, and says he tells them black is a political term.
234.q: Well they haven't really had to face up to it too much yet you know. It hasn't been too much of a problem because they've been going to a school that's, well the people are not really unprejudice, but at the same time they are less prejudice because they have enough money to send their children to…

234.t: Conditioning and prejudice: stories of parents teaching racism
234.s: Gil, Johnston and Anita trade stories of parents teaching racial fear and prejudice, and Gil sums it up as conditioning.
234.q: I had a guy tell me that his mother, said his mother took him and the boys that he grew up with, his friends, who worked for the family, they were rich and lived in ( ? ). He was an arranger with Claude Thornhill, he got drafted and I replaced him. The

150.s: Tex describes black shoppers barred from trying on hats and lacking bathrooms downtown in the 1940s and 50s.
150.q: Well, the Palace was probably the more popular. It was the larger theater, in a sense. And the, I don't know, people sort of relished going downtown New Orleans because they gave them a chance to shop at the end of the stores on Canal Street, even though at that time in history, a lot of blacks…

165.t: Father's teaching that all are God's children; singing a song for money
165.s: His father taught universal brotherhood; as a teen he sang 'Object of My Affection' and later realized why people tossed money.
165.ch: Art Tatum, race and family philosophy
165.q: Oh, yes. That’s going to be interesting. I’m dredging up things that I had completely forgotten about you know. Like I forgot that I had worked with Art Tatum until I started to think about this book. I never told anybody that. I forgot about it. And there’s one really funny incident that I…

1.t: Society rivalries, colour prejudice and hidden kin
1.s: Societies excluded people by skin tone and hair, and Barker adds a story of relatives unknowingly courting each other.
1.q: There was rivalries. Everybody was proud of themselves. We got people that wants to be isolated from other people and they’re particular about who they associate with. Like in our case they had many reasons why they didn’t want to associate with you. A little comedy comes in there. Maybe your lip’s…

144.t: Barred from the University of Detroit; riding in the trunk to Pepper's house
144.s: Fuller was turned away at the Catholic U of D, had lessons downtown, and hid in a car trunk to visit Pepper Adams.
144.q: Fred Mergy, this guy that played like Rosolino or better. The were Catholic over there at the University of Detroit. They didn't have any black kids over there. They finally got one, and they made a basketball star one everybody was pressed to have a black athlete. I forget his name, but he married…

576.t: Racial prejudice in Detroit and the high school principal
576.s: She saw race riots, identified with her Black friends, and was told by her principal not to associate with 'colored girls'.
576.q: Good and bad. Terrible. It was… So again, getting back to the racial prejudice, I didn‟t know it existed until I got to Detroit. I mean, I guess I was kinda like naïve, you‟d say, you know. But I didn‟t know it existed, and then I got to Detroit and I saw what was going on. „Cause as a young kid, I…

400.t: Color prejudice, the Blue Vein Society and winning the junior music scholarship
400.s: Hinton describes color divisions among black Chicagoans, being the only dark child at the Junior Musical Association, and his mother insisting he go back and win the scholarship.
400.ch: Vicksburg, family and the move to Chicago
400.q: “Why can‟t you be nice like Nathaniel”? And I couldn‟t stand him [laugher], because he was nice. He was [unintelligible] my mother… his father, Nat‟s father in Chicago had a little storefront church and my mother played the VYP [unintelligible] young peoples [unintelligible] at five o‟clock in the…

65.t: When he first felt discrimination in Cuba
65.s: His father's wealth shielded him until he started working with Maria Teresa at the Academia El Encanto, where musicians were kept from mixing with the clientele.
65.q: Well, when I was seventeen. I never had, never feel the pressure because I - we don't have - I don't have to work to live. I went to school with the Prio Socarras brothers, the small ones. We went to a private school. I had no problems. My economy liberate me. Like it always happen in every…

26.t: Snubbed by Howard University girls at Murray's Casino
26.s: Greer describes colour and class prejudice among Washington's Black elite and the humiliation of being refused dances.
26.q: Washington, D. C., all them pretty girls from all over the country used to go to Howard University, man, a guy We're dirt like me and you, we nothing. We're nothing. If you Wasn't a doctor or some of that crap, or if you wasn't real bad, you ain't got a chance. We'd be too dark for them.

125.t: Refused service at a restaurant: his father and the color line
125.s: A restaurant manager turned away Thompson and his light-skinned father; this started his thinking about racial strife.
125.q: Specific. Not only just a black boy but a light complected black boy, of a father who looked like a white man. My father did look like a white man, in fact he had more white look than anybody else. In fact it was during this time my father took me into a restaurant he'd been going in for several…
